INTRODUCTION 

The  Parish  of  Manchester  as  it  existed  during  the  period  covered 
by  the  first  volume  of  the  Registers  was  an  extensive  one,  having  an 
area  of  about  fifty  square  miles.  The  town  was  even  then  recognized 
as  a  great  business  centre.  Leland  writing  in  1538  described  it  as 
**  The  fairest,  best  buildid,  quikkest,  and  most  populus  tounne  of  al 
Lancastreshire;  yet  is  in  hit  but  one  paroch  chirch,  but  is  a  College 
and  almost  throughout  doble  ilyd,  ex  quadrato  /apide  durissitnoy 
whereof  a  goodly  quarre  is  harde  by  the  Towne." 

The  parish  and  collegiate  church  which  Leland  saw  is  now  the 
cathedral  church  of  the  Diocese  of  Manchester  as  well  as  the  parish 
church  of  the  very  restricted  cathedral  parish. 

The  old  parish  church  of  Manchester  was  dedicated  to  St  Mary. 
In  142 1  Thomas  La  Warr,  lord  of  the  Manor  of  Manchester  and 
rector  of  the  parish,  obtained  a  licence  to  erect  the  parish  church 
into  a  collegiate  church  and  to  appropriate  for  its  support  the 
revenues  of  the  parish  church  and  parcels  of  the  manor.  The 
coUegiation  was  completed  in  1422,  the  collegiate  body  consisting 
of  a  keeper  or  master  [i.e.  the  warden],  eight  fellows  chaplains, 
four  clerks  and  six  choristers.  The  collegiate  church  was  dedicated 
to  St  Mary,  St  Denis  and  St  George.  In  1547  .the  college  was  dis- 
solved and  the  college  house  (now  Chetham's  Hospital  and  Library) 
and  some  of  the  lands  were  sold  to  the  Earl  of  Derby.  In  1553  the 
college  was  refounded  by  Queen  Mary.  In  1578  the  foundation  was 
dissolved  and  Queen  Elizabeth  granted  the  collie,  under  the  desig- 
nation of  the  Collie  of  Christ,  a  new  charter  which  remained  in 
force  until  1638,  when  Charles  I  granted  another  charter.  Under 
the  charter  of  1638  the  college  was  governed,  with  the  exception  of 
the  period  of  disestablishment  during  the  Commonwealth,  until  the 
19th  century.  In  1840  an  Act  of  Parliament  changed  the  title  of 
the  "Warden  and  Fellows"  to  "Dean  and  Canons."  In  1847  ^^ 
the  foundation  of  the  see  of  Manchester  the  "  Old  Church,"  as  it  had 
been  familiarly  called  for  over  a  century,  became  the  Cathedral. 

B.  M.  b 


viii  INTRODUCTION 

The  clergy  connected  with  the  college  have  been  numerous,  and 
a  few  of  them  were  distinguished  men.  Lives  of  the  wardens  and 
fellows  will  be  found  in  the  publications  of  the  Chetham  Society, 
N.s.  5,  6,  21  and  23,  and  a  general  history  of  the  college  in  Hibbert 
Ware's  Foundations  in  Manchester, 

The  Manchester  Registers,  including  as  they  do  not  only  the 
whole  of  the  baptisms,  burials  and  marriages  of  the  inhabitants  of 
the  central  and  most  populous  part  of  the  parish,  but  also  many  from 
the  outlying  chapelries  and  the  adjoining  parishes,  have  more  than 
the  usual  interest. 

The  Registers  commence  in  1573.  This  is  so  much  later  than 
the  order  (1538)  which  originated  our  parish  registers,  that  we  may 
be  certain  that  the  first  20  or  30  years  of  the  Register  have  been 
lost.  This  is  no  recent  loss  as  is  shown  by  the  memorandum  of 
1693  quoted  later. 

The  oldest  extant  volume  of  the  Registers  is  a  transcript  made  in 
1600  in  compliance  with  an  ordinance  respecting  registers  made  by 
the  Convocation  of  Canterbury  in  1597  and  subsequently  embodied 
in  the  70th  canon  of  1603.  By  the  ordinance  each  parish  was  to 
provide  itself  with  a  parchment  book  in  which  the  entries  from  the 
old  paper  books  were  to  be  fairly  and  legibly  transcribed.  From  the 
beginning  the  registers  of  baptisms,  marriages  and  burials  have,  in 
Manchester,  been  kept  separate  and  not  mixed  as  in  many  parishes, 
but  for  almost  a  couple  of  centuries  the  three  registers  were  bound 
together. 

The  Registers  consist  of  (i)  the  Registers  proper,  (2)  Paper  Books, 
(3)  Sexton's  Books,  and  (4)  "  Indexes." 

(i)  Registers  Proper. 

The  following  is  a  list  of  the  first  class  with  references  to  such  of 
the  others  as  supplement  the  Register. 

As  the  volumes  are  not  numbered  I  have  given  each  a  number  or 
title  and  number  in  square  brackets,  in  addition  to  the  present 
lettering,  which  is  often  inaccurate.

INTRODUCTION  xi 

Volume  I.  is  the  volume  here  printed.  It  consists  of  257  leaves 
of  parchment. 

Volume  II.  begins  "A  Register  booke  provided  by  y*  Curche 
[sic]  wardens  of  this  prnte  yeares  of  our  Lorde  God  16 16  and  161 7." 

Volume  III.  illustrates  at  its  best  the  system  of  civil  registration 
adopted  during  the  Protectorate.  Births  instead  of  baptisms  are 
recorded  and  the  details  as  to  parentage  and  condition  of  bride- 
grooms and  brides  are  almost  as  full  as  under  our  present  system. 
The  Manchester  Registers  in  the  Commonwealth  period  are  indeed 
a  joy  to  genealogists.  This  volume  was  lost  for  very  many  years, 
probably  sixty.  It  was  missing  when  John  Palmer  made  his  extracts 
and  also  in  1831  when  the  "Parish  Register  Abstract "  was  compiled. 
In  1843  it  was  discovered  in  the  office  of  Messrs  Cooke,  Beever  and 
Darwell,  Attomeys-at-Law,  and  by  them  restored  to  the  collegiate 
church. 

Volume  IV.  **  A  Register  Booke  provided  by  the  Churchwardens 
for  the  yeare  of  our  Lord  God  1662  and  1663"  has  the  following 
note  on  the  first  page : — 

"  No.  2,  1693. 

Memorandum,  y'  y*  Register  Books  belonging  to  y«  Church  of  Man- 
chester were  upon  y*  death  of  Mr  John  Newton  late  parish  dark 
called  for  and  examined  by  y*  Warden  Dr  Wroe  and  [found]  to  be 
all  there  and  complete  and  perfect,  viz.:  4  Books  [of]  Parch- 
ment, and  one  in  paper  for  burying  in  Woollen.  Witness  my 
hand  Ric.  Wroe  Warden  of  Manchester." 
The  books  mentioned  would  be  Volumes  I.  II.  III.  IV.  and  V., 

and  this  shows  that  as  early  as  1693  the  Registers  prior  to  1573  were 

no  longer  in  existence. 

Volume  VI.  **  A  Register  Book  provided  by  the  Church  Wardens 

for  the  year  of  our  Lord  God  1701  and   1702"  also  contains  a 

memorandum  by  Warden  Wroe.

complete  and  perfect,  viz.:  5  Books  in  Parchment,  and  one  in

was  superseded  in  171 1,  is  Vol.  V.  and  is  still  in  good  condition. 
Volume  VII.,  lettered  1728 — 1791,  really  contains  entries  to  March 
1738 — 9  only.  At  the  end,  however,  is  entered  "  An  Account  of  the 
Births  and  Burials  of  the  children  of  Thomas  Butterworth  Bayley 
Esquire  of  Hope,  etc."  dated  "Hope  October  4th  1783,"  but  con- 
taining later  entries.  As  many  of  Bayley's  children  were  baptized  by 
Nonconformist  ministers  this  was  probably  his  means  of  getting  their 
names  placed  on  public  record. 

Where  the  volumes  of  the  Register  overlap  it  is  by  no  means  to 
be  taken  for  granted  that  the  entries  of  that  period  are  identical.  In 
Vol.  III.  1662,  Mar.  28,  is  the  burial  of  *^John  Benson  of  Man- 
chester." Vol.  IV.  under  the  same  date  records  the  burial  of  **  John 
Benson  of  Manchester  shoemaker.'*  The  addition  of  the  trade  might 
be  essential  to  identification.

(2)  Paper  Books. 

The  Paper  Books  are  the  books  in  which  events  were  entered  as 
they  occunred  to  be  subsequently  copied  into  the  Register  proper. 
The  Register  proper  is  legal  evidence,  and  it  has  been  decided  that 
documents  like  the  Paper  Books  are  merely  private  memoranda  and 
are  not  admissible  as  evidence.  Nevertheless,  whatever  they  may  be 
technically,  the  Paper  Books  are  in  fact  very  important  evidence,  and 
having  been  written  up  at  the  actual  time  of  the  event  are  really 
better  evidence  than  the  Register  proper.  The  entries  in  the  Paper 
Books  are  very  often  fuller  than  the  same  entries  in  the  Register 
proper.  At  one  period  the  Paper  Book  invariably  gave  the  street 
address  (e.g.  Deansgate)  of  persons  named  in  the  entries  while  the 
corresponding  entries  in  the  Register  proper  give  only  the  town 
"  Manchester."  As  further  illustrations  of  the  value  of  the  Paper 
Books  a  couple  of  extracts  may  be  given,  the  additional  information 
in  the  Paper  Book  being  given  in  brackets. 

"  1696,  Aug.  7,  Sarah  wife  to  Ralph   Pycroft  of  ManC  [Buried 
beehinde  Warrington] 

1696,  Sep.  14,  Richard  Booth  of  Manch'  [Orgenest]." 

In  the  Paper  Books  groups  of  entries  are  often  out  of  chrono- 
logical order.  In  the  following  schedule  these  groups  are  numbered 
in  the  order  in  which  they  occur  in  each  volume.

(3)  Sexton's  Books. 

Another  series  of  valuable  records  consists  of  the  Sexton's  Books. 
These  are  volumes  in  which  the  sexton  recorded  not  only  the  names 
of  persons  buried  but  also  particulars  as  to  fees,  ages  and  causes 
of  death.  The  Registers  proper  do  not  give  ages  at  death  before 
1 81 3  while  the  Sexton's  Books  give  them  sixty  years  earlier.

xvi  INTRODUCTION 


(4)   '^  Index." 

The  last  series  of  Registers  is  that  called  the  "Index."  The 
"  Index "  is  a  chronological  copy  of  the  Register,  but  most  of  the 
earlier  volumes  styled  the  "  Index  "  appear  to  me  to  be  the  Register 
proper,  as  they  are  the  only  registers  for  the  period  complying  with 
the  Canon  of  1603  by  being  on  parchment.  As  such  they  are  included 
in  the  first  schedule.  The  first  of  the  "  Indexes  "  other  than  those 
which  are  really  Registers  proper,  is  of  marriages  from  1754.  As 
there  are  many  entries  on  a  page  it  is  easier  to  find  any  particular 
marriage  by  the  "  Index  '*  than  by  turning  over  the  pages  of  the 
Register  containing  the  forms  on  which  marriages  were  entered 
under  the  1753  Act.  Apart  from  the  "Indexes'*  of  marriages,  the 
other  so-called  "  Indexes "  are  really  Registers  proper  until  the  Act 
of  181 2  came  into  force. 

The  Registers  are  safely  and  commodiously  housed  in  the 
Registry  of  the  Cathedral.  Thanks  are  due  to  the  Right  Rev. 
Bishop  Welldon,  Dean  of  the  Cathedral,  and  to  the  churchwardens 
of  Manchester  for  their  kind  permission  to  print  the  Registers,  and 
to  the  Rev.  A.  C.  Keene,  B.D.,  Clerk  in  Orders,  Mr  C.  W.  Sutton,  M.  A., 
the  Senior  Churchwarden,  and  Mr  Alfred  Wilson,  the  Verger,  for  the 
very  courteous  manner  in  which  they  have  facilitated  the  revision  of 
the  transcript  Mr  Sutton,  in  his  other  capacity  of  Chief  Librarian 
and,  as  such,  custodian  of  John  Owen's  transcript,  has  taken  an  active 
interest  in  the  work  throughout. 

The  late  John  Owen  transcribed  the  whole  of  the  marriages  from 
the  beginning  in  1573— -1804,  the  baptisms  to  1751  and  the  burials 
to  1750,  and  subsequently  made  a  fresh  copy,  the  entries  being  in 
alphabetical  (not  lexicographical)  order.  These  two  transcripts,  with 
a  copy  of  part  of  the  Sexton's  Books  and  copies  of  all  the  inscriptions 
in  the  Cathedral  and  formerly  in  the  graveyard,  are  now  preserved 
amongst  the  Owen  MSS.  in  the  Reference  Library,  Manchester. 
Though  not  without  errors  Owen's  transcripts,  especially  the  alpha- 
betical one,  are  invaluable  as  affording  a  ready  clue  to  the  contents 
of  the  Registers.  They  are,  of  course,  freely  accessible  to  all  who 
desire  to  use  them. 

Though  Manchester  had  only  one  Parish  Church  there  were  in 
the  parish  a  number  of  chapels  more  or  less  autonomous  and  with 
registers  of  their  own.     These  chapelries  were  as  follows  and  had.

xviii  INTRODUCTION 

It  having  been  announced  that  I  was  to  edit  this  volume,  I  may 
be  allowed  a  word  of  explanation. 

A  typed  copy  of  John  Owen's  transcript  was  the  basis  of  the 
present  volume.  It  had  been  my  intention  to  compare  this  transcript 
with  the  original  and  to  have  a  volume  ready  for  publication  in  the 
course  of  two  or  three  years.  I  had  reckoned  without  Mr  Brierley. 
Instead  of  waiting  my  leisure,  Mr  Brierley,  assisted  by  Mrs  Brierley 
and  Miss  Wrigley,  took  the  whole  of  the  revision,  proof-reading  and 
indexing  in  hand,  and  before  I  saw  a  proof  the  whole  of  the  work 
was  done,  and  the  editor  that  was  to  have  been  had  no  opportunity 
of  doing  anything  except  writing  the  introduction  and  thanking  his 
Wigan  friends.  Josiah  Arrowsmith,  probably  the  most  enthusiastic 
member  of  our  Society  and  its  valued  auditor,  was  looking  forward  to 
taking  the  lion's  share  of  the  work  of  revision  of  the  Manchester 
Registers  when  death  removed  a  gentle,  lovable  man  and  a  most 
painstaking  and  unassuming  worker  for  the  Lancashire  Parish 
Register  Society.

Where  a  name  has  variants  the  Head -name  has  been  selected  which  now 
exists  or  which  most  closely  resembles  the  modern  equivalent.  All  variants  are 
separately  Indexed  with  cross  references  to  the  Head-name. 

Where  a  Surname  has  an  cUias  each  form  of  the  Surname  is  Indexed  under  its 
initial  letter. 

The  Christian  names  are,  with  some  few  exceptions,  Indexed  under  their 
modem  form — the  first  spelling  of  the  name  having  generally  been  continued 
in  connection  with  the  same  Surname. 

Illegitimate  children  are  Indexed  under  the  Surnames  of  both  Mother  and 
putative  Father. 

"N.X.N."  signifies  "No  Christian  Name." 

An  Asterisk  following  a  page  number  signifies  that  that  combination  of 
Christian  and  Surname  occurs  more  than  once  on  the  page  number  asterisked. 

Note,     Reference  should  also  be  made  to  the  Corrigenda.
